Once you get straight what you are asking Distance to compute, hopefully the errors will evaporate, and you can ask your next set of questions about interpretation of results. messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am working with line transect data collected from wild long-tailed macaques from 2 different strata.

1) The data set I am having a problem with is composed of 35 observations (23 in stratum 1 and 12 in stratum 2). I have selected 10% right truncation and manually pooled the data into 5 intervals. However, when I run the analysis, my observations are reduced to 18 and 10, respectively. A total of 7 observations have been omitted. Is there something I might have done unknowingly to further right truncate the data? The left truncation is set to 0 and I can't figure out how 10% truncation resulted in omitting 7/35 observations.

2) I also had one more question about survey effort. The value generated by Distance for one of the strata seems abnormally low.
The total distance walked for each grid was:

B1 - 79.2 km
B2 - 68.2 km

Each grid had a strip width of 39m. The effort, however, was:

B1 - 5200
B2 - 9700

Is it normal for the effort to contradict the distance walked per transect? I would have expected the effort to be higher in B1 since we walked an extra 10+ km over the course of the year.

Thank you all for your help. I have tried to find faculty at my institution that are familiar with Distance to no avail. I'm very grateful for this group.

Best,
Lauren

messages.subject: using additional ("transit-leg") sightings in the detection function, but not in estimating density
messages.subject_clean: using additional ("transit-leg") sightings in the detection function, but not in estimating density
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
When studying rare species, it can be difficult to collect enough sightings to fit a detection function reliably.  I recently did a systematic, small-boat line transect survey for marine mammals.  Observers stayed on effort and collected sightings on both planned (designed) transects and along transit legs.  I’m trying to conduct an analysis in Distance 6.2 (Release 1) in which I use all sightings for fitting the detection function, but only the effort and sightings from the planned transects for estimating encounter rate and density.  I am not sure whether this gets done in Distance using data filters (i.e., I have coded the data so that all of the “transit-leg” sightings were assigned to a transect called Transect 0, so maybe I should be filtering Transect>0 for estimating density), or stratification (i.e., I have set up a “planned” stratum and a “transit-leg” stratum — and maybe I should simply ignore the abundance in the transit-leg stratum).

This is slightly embarrassing, because I’ve written about this in previous collaborative studies, but in both cases, the analyses were done by co-authors who are statisticians doing the analyses in R.  In one, we had extra sightings, but we also had so few sightings that we had poor power to choose among models.  In that case, we used the extra sightings, but also model averaged on the detection function (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0006320709000500 ).  In another case, the primary purpose was to collect ID photos and biopsy samples, so having much more search effort in the high-density area than the low-density area required us to use density surface models (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1523-1739.2011.01656.x/abstract) <http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1523-1739.2011.01656.x/abstract?userIsAuthenticated=false&deniedAccessCustomisedMessage=>.

The current study used a systematic survey design, but it was an inefficient one.  We have so many transit-leg sightings that we have to use them to have any hope of estimating esw.  It’s important for this study that we do the analysis in Distance, because we want to share the data and Distance project with other Distance users.  I’ve searched in the Google Group help pages for “transit-leg” sightings, “extra” sightings, “additional” sightings…  I can’t find anything, so I know I’m overlooking something obvious.  I have a vague recollection of this coming up in the context of the pooling robustness properties of distance sampling in the context of stratified surveys, but that workshop was many years ago and I don’t know how to tell Distance to use all sightings for fitting the detection function, but only a subset for estimating abundance.

Thanks in advance for your help,
Rob

messages.body_plain:
Lauren

You are below a reasonable number of samples for fitting your detection functions with the original 35 detections.  Moving on from that, I suspect the reason that exactly 3 or 4 detections (~10% of 35) is because having converted your exact distances to binned distances as a result of your 'manual pooling', the 10% most distant detections lies inside perhaps your final bin.  The entire bin will be excluded as a result of the truncation.  With 35 sightings it will be easy to check whether that is the case.  With larger sample sizes, and no binning, the percentage of sightings removed because of truncation may not be exactly 10% because of multiple sightings at the same distance.  But your small sample size and manual binning will exaggerate that effect.

As for your second question about effort, I need more information.  I understand that you say you walked the two distances in km.  I don't know where in the Distance output you plucked the second set of numbers, nor the units in which those numbers are expressed.  Perhaps you could provide more detailed program output.  How many transects per stratum, the length of each transect, perhaps the number of repeat walks of the transects?

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] repeated transects in dsm
messages.body_plain:
Natalia

You raise some useful issues.  However two of your statements seem inconsistent with each other "I am interested in annual density, not in density by time periods" and "could be a change in density between periods".  If statement 2 is true, then statement 1 is in doubt.

Commonly, repeat visits are used to produce sufficient detections to reliably estimate the detection function.  Pooling data across visits produces an estimate of average density/abundance across visits.

If you do pool the visits, then you should multiply effort by the number of visits.  In the case of density surface modelling, the effort that is relevant is the size of the segments into which the transects have been cut.  The response variable being modelled by the density surface is something akin to number of animals inside a segment after adjusting for imperfect detectability.  If the repeated visits is not incorporated into the transect length (and hence into the segment lengths), this response variable will not be correct.

You raise a good point about temporal correlation.  Spatio-temporal models (see email to this list from Dave Miller on 29 March 2016) could address this, but as Dave says, this is still is the 'experimental' stage.

I hope that is of some use to you.

messages.subject: Obsever Experience
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

I was interested to know if any of you have used observer experience as a covariate in your distance model.  Particularly, I am interested in how you chose to quantify experience and whether this was a useful covariate or not.

We fly helicopter-based line transect surveys for quail and employ 3 observers plus the pilot.  We have noticed that in some surveys with multiple new observers (2 or more) that our detection probability is much lower closer to the transect line (0-10m).  This problem doesn't seem to appear nearly ever with experienced observers.

Any information on this subject is most appreciated regardless of survey type or species.

Thanks,

John Edwards

messages.subject: Re: Obsever Experience
messages.body_plain:
We looked at this question using a 20-yr, large scale riparian bird community monitoring project with multiple observers with various levels of experience.  Using #of field seasons with the project there was a modest effect on overall densities (due to differences in mean distances), more of an effect on diversity metrics from total #field seasons (from applications that were kept on file).  But there were very large differences between even equally experiences observers.  Ultimately we felt it all had to come out in the wash through good study design & implementation.  For example, we used the analysis argue for shifting to a spatially balanced design (did not happen), got serious about randomly rotating observers, and got very serious about our training program (or programme, as this is an international listserv...).  There is systematic variance you can control for, model the effects of, or assume away.  But we never did publish anything on it.

Cheers -

Russ Norvell
Avian Conservation Program Coordinator
Utah Division of Wildlife Resources

messages.subject_clean: Port existing Distance 6 or Distance 7 projects to R
messages.body_plain:
Group friends

Do you have projects you have built in Distance 6 or Distance 7? Are you
curious about analysing these distance sampling surveys using R?  If so,
we have some news.

Dave Miller has developed an R package called 'readdst'.  The purpose of
this package is to read Distance projects (these projects as you know
use the '.dst' extension, hence the name readdst). Distance projects
effectively store not only data, but also model definitions and data
filters in Access-like databases.  Dave's package reads these databases
and converts the data to forms readable by R as well as calls to the
'mrds' package for fitting detection functions and producing abundance
estimates.

The 'readdst' package does not live on CRAN, but you can install it to
your R installation from its Github repository via the function
'install_github()' in the devtools package.

library(devtools)
install_github("DistanceDevelopment/readdst")

A case study showing the use of 'readdst' is available on the
'distancesampling.org <http://distancesampling.org>' website, along with other vignettes for analysing
distance data in R.

Look at the bottom of this distancesampling.org <http://distancesampling.org> page
http://distancesampling.org/R/index.html under 'Migrating data and
analyses from Distance for Windows to R environment'.

The 'readdst' package has limitations; it cannot properly migrate
projects that use multipliers or post-stratification.  It does not cope
with 'dsm', 'mads' or 'DSsim' projects.

We welcome your feedback.

I may be way off base here, but much head scratching and research has led me to seek the advice from this wise group.

Basic background:

Fish count data (with covariates) from line transect sampling via manned submersible.

Any suggestions for alternatives?  I keep scratching my head thinking of how I can tie together all of these pieces I have.

I hope this relatively clear to understand! I truly appreciate any help and/or suggestions. Something about bringing this all together just isn't clicking for me!

Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Katy, list

DSM is not really my thing, but here are some comments. Hope I didn't miss the point entirely ;)

You do not need the coordinates of the individuals per se. But you need some minimal data related to location. You don't have the coordinates for each observation, but I assume you can put them into "boxes" (i.e. transect segments) given your constant speed? If that is the case then you should be able to implement a DSM, since the spatial modelling happens at the "box" level, not at the individual observation level. The only modelling that goes on at the individual level is regarding detectability, but for that I assume you have the relevant covariates for each observation.

I also assume you have the habitat covariate (and any other(s) going into the DSM) over the entire area you might want your inferences to apply to? As that would be required for the prediction stage, i.e. naturally you do not need the covariates for the DSM on the transects only, but everywhere else.

People have typically used equal size boxes to do the modelling, but I don't see why one might not use unequal size boxes (if say, because, as in your case, useful covariates to explain density appear in discrete patches) as long as due care is taken regarding properly accounting for the size of the box via the offset. There might be unforeseen problems if some boxes are much larger than others. Also not sure if the existing packages to implement DSMs can deal with that off the shelf or would you have to tweak them / code it yourself.

Hope this helps, but DSM folks might have more ideas/thoughts

cheers

Tiago

As Tiago says, your effort needs to be defined at the segment (hist term 'box') level.  The key point is that you are able to properly assign your detections to the segment in which it belongs. Olá Jorge, list ;)

(sorry folks for the "patriotic" wording above, but It's good to get Portuguese questions in this forum, not that often it happens!)

Regarding the questions:

- To the best of my knowledge in these R packages cluster size has to be included in the analysis as a covariate, no option for using size bias regression.

- implementation details apart, but I'm assuming this is possible in dsm, you can use a pooled detection function across years to predict density on a year by year basis in a DSM. However, you have to ask yourself the following: does it make sense that you do not have enough detections to estimate a detection function per year, which typically has a small number of parameters associated with, but then you have enough data to estimate a density surface model each year, which probably requires more parameters to specify any way? I guess you could fit a common model across years (so really a spatio-temporal model) which includes variables which change each year, hence borrowing strength across years using a pooled model that then is used to make predictions per year, but I'm not sure that is possible off the shelf in dsm (and my first guess would be no...) so that might not be something you want to get into to begin with.

I hope this helps, others feel free to add

cheers

T

Just to follow-up on Tiago's answers...

- The current set of R packages don't have any functions to perform the
size-bias regression (though it is, of course, possible to code this up

observation data frame to ensure that only the correct detections are
included (dsm may complain about this, if it does drop me an e-mail).
I'll echo Tiago's comments, that building a separate model per year
discards the possible information between years, even if you have lots
of data. That being said, building a fully spatiotemporal model in dsm
is still experimental -- in the sense that we don't have good advice on
what form the model should take in particular situations (and there are
many possible modelling options). See e.g. this thread:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/distance-sampling/fvjVYQIn4kw/9FwzGsWcCQAJ

Hope this helps!

Mirium and Haris (list)

The submission of your two questions within an hour of each other leads me to suspect the two questions might be related, so I will deal with them in the same response.

These questions remind us of the rule that we cannot do a proper analysis without considering the survey design.  We do not know how many transects were sampled (output below suggests 11), nor the number of visits made per year.  Without those details, precise advice about analysis will be difficult to give.

Fortunately Mirium provided her data in the form of a spreadsheet.  From the transect label data, it appears in her situation there are 4 locations, three locations having 14 transects, the other having 11 transects.  It also appears that the transects were visited multiple times each year over the period 2009-2012.  She has also recorded species, cluster size, perpendicular distance, and a few other things.

The main cause of perceived over-estimation of density is failure to properly describe survey effort.  Mirium's spreadsheet shows all the detections.  What it does not show are visits to transects where no birds were seen.  For distance sampling, emphasis is upon sampling effort rather than the detections (of course the detections are important).

To produce reasonable estimates of density, a fundamental quantity needed is encounter rate (number of detections per unit of effort).  If the effort is mis-specified, then encounter rate will be wrong; specifically, if survey effort is specified as too small (not accounting for transect visits when no detections were made), then encounter rate will be improperly large, and consequently the estimate of density will be too large.

To organise your data in such a way that Distance can make sense of your survey design, I recommend the following.  There are more clever ways of doing this, but this might be the most simple.

Create 16 strata from your data: one for each location x year combination; e.g. Anam09 ... Anam12, Nell09 ... Nell12, Para09 ... Para12, Vaz09 ... Vaz12

Within each strata, list all 14 (or 11 transects); in the effort (or line length) field, multiply line length (1km) by the number of visits in the given year.  There will be a row in your datasheet for each sighting in that location x year combination indicating the transect on which the sighting was made.  Should there have been a transect on which there were no sightings on any visit, that transect (and its total length) must be present with the perpendicular distance column BLANK (to properly account for survey effort expended).

Use a data filter to use only the data for species 1 (GHB), then in your analysis, request a stratified estimate, resulting in 16 estimates; one for each location x year combination.  Repeat for the next species (MGH).  Note that species MPH was inly sighted in your fourth location (Vazhachal-shola) and there were only 42 detections, making fitting a detection function troublesome.

Finally, note that your perpendicular distance data will be problematic for producing suitable fits of detection functions (see histograms below).  My belief is that your hornbills were detecting you before you detected them and they were creeping away from the transect prior to detection.  I say this because for each location (pooled across years and species) there is a distinct lack of detections at distances <5m from the transect.  Conventional distance sampling assumes detection of all hornbills on the transect and a smooth declining number of detections as perpendicular distance increases.  Hence, fitting a half-normal detection function to these data may be the appropriate thing to do, but goodness of fit statistics will suggest the model does not fit.

messages.body_plain:
Stewart

Readers of this list who are not interested in georeferenced coordinates on the surface of the earth, look away now.

Yes, there have been a few changes to the example project of the Gulf of Mexico spotted dolphins; but I believe x and y have been present in the R example data since Miller et al. (2013) MEE paper described the analysis.  The standalone Distance project used latitude and longitude of segment centres, not taking account of the inequality of a degree of latitude and a degree of longitude.

There were two transformations performed upon both the segment and prediction grid data.  Remember any covariates that appear at the segment layer and subsequently used in your prediction model, will need to be present in your prediction grid.  Lat/long was converted to UTMs to solve the asymmetry of degrees of lat/long.  Secondly, Miller centred the UTMs on the centroid of the study area so the values were more compatible.  Notice that the vignette and wiki you cite in your email both use "x" and "y" and predictors having made these adjustments.  As such, the "latitude" and "longitude" variables are redundant and not used in the analyses, and could have been deleted.

If you are working with a small-ish study area, then lat/long is probably not a sensible coordinate system in which to record your data.  The modest GIS inside standalone Distance can transform lat/long to UTMs, but it cannot centre the coordinates.  Centring is unlikely to make vast differences to your analysis, but because spatial models can do curious things, centring provides some protection from some of those curiosities.

messages.body_plain:
Ana

I suspect the error is not coming about as a result of your data filter, but rather as a result of your use of the "special" Detected field (that you have renamed Seen) being text rather than numeric.

Note this passage from the Users Guide:

Double observer data has two fields that can be used in conjunction with the data selection options in the Data Filter to achieve the desired analysis. The two fields are observer (which is 1 for the first observer and 2 for the second) and detected (which is 1 if the animal was detected by that observer and 0 if not; note that the actual field names may be different from this).
The passage notes that you can change the field names, but there in no indication you can change the field contents (or type).

My advice is to change your fields Y=>1, N=>0 and specify the field is of type integer when imported.

Ana

I suspect the error is not coming about as a result of your data filter, but rather as a result of your use of the "special" Detected field (that you have renamed Seen) being text rather than numeric.

Note this passage from the Users Guide:

Double observer data has two fields that can be used in conjunction with the data selection options in the Data Filter to achieve the desired analysis. The two fields are observer (which is 1 for the first observer and 2 for the second) and detected (which is 1 if the animal was detected by that observer and 0 if not; note that the actual field names may be different from this).

The passage notes that you can change the field names, but there in no indication you can change the field contents (or type).

My advice is to change your fields Y=>1, N=>0 and specify the field is of type integer when imported.
